title: Gas exchange: partial pressures and diffusion
goal: Explain how partial pressures drive O₂ and CO₂ across the lung, why arterial O₂ stays high in most people during exercise, and why some highly trained athletes become hypoxaemic.

steps.title: Partial pressure: each gas pushes on its own
steps.text:
Air is a mix of gases. Each one exerts its own [partial pressure](g:partial-pressure), and together they add up to the total pressure (Dalton's law) [[c:dalton]]. A gas's partial pressure is its fraction × the total.

At sea level the total is 760 mmHg and O₂ is 20.9% of dry air, so air's PO₂ is about **159 mmHg**. In the alveoli it is lower, about **104 mmHg**, while PCO₂ is about **40 mmHg** [[c:alveolar-gas]]. The airways humidify the air, and alveolar air holds more CO₂ and less O₂ than outside air [[c:alveolar-mix]].

This course gives pressures in mmHg. Divide by 7.5 for kPa: 104 mmHg ≈ 13.9 kPa, 40 mmHg ≈ 5.3 kPa.

claims.text: Each gas in a mixture exerts its own partial pressure; the total pressure is their sum. At sea level air is 20.9% O₂, a PO₂ of 158.8 of 760 mmHg.

evidence.quote: Total pressure is the sum of all the partial pressures of a gaseous mixture.

Dalton’s law describes the behavior of nonreactive gases in a gaseous mixture and states that a specific gas type in a mixture exerts its own pressure; thus, the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the partial pressures of the gases in the mixture.
Partial Pressures of Atmospheric Gases. Oxygen (O₂): percent of total composition 20.9, partial pressure (mm Hg) 158.8.

claims.text: Alveolar PO₂ is about 104 mmHg and alveolar PCO₂ about 40 mmHg.

evidence.quote: The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg
The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood of the capillary is about 45 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the alveoli is about 40 mm Hg.

claims.text: Alveolar air holds more water vapour and CO₂ and less O₂ than atmospheric air.

evidence.quote: Recall that the respiratory system works to humidify incoming air, thereby causing the air present in the alveoli to have a greater amount of water vapor than atmospheric air.
In addition, alveolar air contains a greater amount of carbon dioxide and less oxygen than atmospheric air.

steps.title: The PO₂ of air at sea level
steps.problem: Dry air is 20.9% O₂. At sea level the total (barometric) pressure is 760 mmHg. What is the PO₂ of the air?
steps: Turn the percentage into a fraction: 20.9% = 0.209.
PO₂ = fraction × total pressure = 0.209 × 760 = 158.8 mmHg, about 159 mmHg.

Once the air is warmed and humidified in the airways, water vapour takes 47 mmHg of the total, so O₂'s share is then taken of 760 − 47 mmHg. That is a different question from the PO₂ of the outside air.

steps.title: Diffusion runs downhill
steps.text:
Gases cross the [respiratory membrane](g:respiratory-membrane) by simple diffusion: from higher to lower partial pressure, and faster when the difference is bigger [[c:diffusion-gradient]].

Blood arriving in a lung capillary has a PO₂ of about 40 mmHg, against 104 mmHg in the alveolus: a 64 mmHg push for O₂. Blood leaving the lung, in the pulmonary veins, is at about 100 mmHg [[c:o2-gradient]].

CO₂ goes the other way, from about 45 mmHg in the blood to 40 mmHg in the alveolus. That is only a 5 mmHg push, yet similar amounts of the two gases cross [[c:co2-gradient]].

claims.text: Gas exchange is simple diffusion down a partial-pressure gradient; a bigger difference gives faster movement.

evidence.quote: A gas will move from an area where its partial pressure is higher to an area where its partial pressure is lower.
In addition, the greater the partial pressure difference between the two areas, the more rapid is the movement of gases.
The actual exchange of gases occurs due to simple diffusion.

claims.text: Alveolar PO₂ is about 104 mmHg against about 40 mmHg in blood arriving in the capillary, a gradient of about 64 mmHg; blood in the pulmonary veins is at about 100 mmHg.

evidence.quote: This difference is about 64 mm Hg: The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is about 104 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the blood of the capillary is about 40 mm Hg.
The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg, whereas the partial pressure of oxygenated blood in pulmonary veins is about 100 mm Hg.

claims.text: The CO₂ gradient is only about 5 mmHg (45 to 40 mmHg), yet similar amounts of O₂ and CO₂ cross.

evidence.quote: However, the partial pressure difference is less than that of oxygen, about 5 mm Hg.
As a result, the relative concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide that diffuse across the respiratory membrane are similar.

steps.title: Why arterial O₂ usually stays high
steps.text:
In exercise, blood flow through the lung rises faster than the capillary blood volume can grow, so each red cell spends less time in the capillary [[c:transit-falls]]. About 0.3–0.4 s is thought to be enough to load it fully. In 16 women and 16 men the average stayed above 0.3 s, even at 90% of peak O₂ uptake [[c:transit-enough]].

Ventilation keeps pace too. In healthy people, alveolar ventilation and diffusion rise in step with metabolic rate, so arterial PO₂ doesn't fall and PCO₂ doesn't rise [[c:matched]].

That is why, in most people, arterial O₂ stays close to resting values even at VO₂max. Some highly trained athletes are the exception.

claims.text: Because cardiac output rises more than pulmonary capillary blood volume, capillary transit time falls progressively with exercise.

evidence.quote: As Q̇ increases with exercise more than capillary blood volume recruitment, mean pulmonary capillary transit time declines progressively with exercise.

claims.text: A transit time of at least 0.3–0.4 s is thought to be needed; in healthy men and women the mean did not drop below 0.3 s up to 90% of peak O₂ uptake.

evidence.quote: It has been suggested that pulmonary capillary transit time must be at least 0.3–0.4 s to allow for adequate red blood cell oxygenation
the mean PTT did not drop below 0.3 s in either group

claims.text: In healthy exercise, alveolar ventilation and alveolar-capillary diffusion rise in proportion to metabolic rate, preventing PaCO₂ from rising and PaO₂ from falling.

evidence.quote: During exercise by healthy mammals, alveolar ventilation and alveolar-capillary diffusion increase in proportion to the increase in metabolic rate to prevent PaCO2 from increasing and PaO2 from decreasing.

steps.title: When arterial O₂ does fall
steps.text:
In 16 highly trained runners (VO₂max 72 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), arterial PO₂ held within 10 mmHg of rest in only four. In eight it fell by 21–35 mmHg, to below 75 mmHg [[c:dempsey-runners]]. This is [exercise-induced arterial hypoxaemia](g:eiah) (EIAH), graded by [SaO₂](g:sao2): mild 93–95%, moderate 88–93%, severe below 88% [[c:eiah-grades]].

Two things usually combine: a wide alveolar-to-arterial PO₂ gap, and too little extra breathing [[c:eiah-causes]]. It is common in the very fit: 70% of highly trained male runners fell to 91% or less on a treadmill [[c:eiah-men]]. Women can show it at lower fitness: in 67% of 52 young women (VO₂max 28–61 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), SaO₂ fell 4% or more on a bike [[c:eiah-women]].

claims.text: In 16 highly trained runners, 4 kept PaO₂ within 10 mmHg of rest, 4 fell 10–15 mmHg and 8 fell 21–35 mmHg, to below 75 mmHg.

evidence.quote: Four runners maintained arterial PO2 (Pa, O2) within 10 mmHg of resting values, another four showed 10-15 mmHg reductions in Pa, O2, and the remaining eight showed reductions of 21-35 mmHg, i.e. in all cases to a Pa, O2 of less than 75 mmHg and to less than 60 mmHg in two cases.

claims.text: Proposed grades of EIAH: mild SaO₂ 93–95% (or 3–4% below rest), moderate 88–93%, severe below 88%.

evidence.quote: we suggest that mild EIAH be defined as an arterial O(2) saturation of 93-95% (or 3-4% <rest), moderate EIAH as 88-93%, and severe EIAH as <88%.

claims.text: An excessive alveolar-to-arterial PO₂ difference and inadequate compensatory hyperventilation commonly combine to cause EIAH.

evidence.quote: Both an excessive alveolar-to-arterial PO(2) difference (A-a DO(2)) (>25-30 Torr) and inadequate compensatory hyperventilation (arterial PCO(2) >35 Torr) commonly contribute to EIAH

claims.text: In highly trained male runners (VO₂max above 68 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), 70% desaturated to 91% or less on a maximal treadmill test.

evidence.quote: 55 of 79 subjects (70%) exhibited exercise-induced arterial desaturation

claims.text: In 52 young women of mixed fitness, 67% showed EIAH (a fall of 4% or more in SaO₂) on a maximal cycle test.

evidence.quote: EIAH was present in 67% of the women

debate.question: What widens the alveolar-to-arterial PO₂ gap in EIAH?

sides.position: Mainly a diffusion limit: in part of the lung, red cells pass through too fast to load fully.
Uneven matching of ventilation to blood flow contributes about as much as diffusion, and how either arises in heavy exercise is still unknown.

points: Each gas exerts its own partial pressure (fraction × total): dry air at sea level has a PO₂ of about 159 mmHg; alveolar air about 104 mmHg O₂ and 40 mmHg CO₂.
O₂ and CO₂ cross the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, down partial-pressure gradients of about 64 mmHg and 5 mmHg.
In exercise, red cells spend less time in lung capillaries, but in most people transit time stays long enough and ventilation keeps pace, so arterial PO₂ holds.
Some highly trained athletes show exercise-induced arterial hypoxaemia: SaO₂ 93–95% mild, 88–93% moderate, below 88% severe.
EIAH usually comes from a wide alveolar-arterial gap plus too little extra breathing; what widens the gap is still debated.

variants.stem: In a lung capillary, which way does O₂ move, and what drives it?

options.text: Into the blood, because alveolar PO₂ is higher
options.why: Right: O₂ diffuses down its gradient, from about 104 mmHg in the alveolus to about 40 mmHg in arriving blood.

options.text: Into the alveolus, because blood holds more O₂
options.why: Blood does hold more O₂ in total, but diffusion follows partial pressure, which is higher in the alveolus.

options.text: Into the blood, pumped across by the membrane
options.why: No pump: gas exchange is simple diffusion down a partial-pressure gradient.

options.text: Both ways equally, so the net flow is zero
options.why: There is a net flow because the partial pressures differ by about 64 mmHg.

variants.stem: During a run, which way does CO₂ move across the alveolar wall, and what drives it?

options.text: Into the alveolus, because blood PCO₂ is higher
options.why: Right: about 45 mmHg in the blood against about 40 mmHg in the alveolus.

options.text: Into the blood, because alveolar air holds more CO₂ than outside air
options.why: Alveolar air does hold more CO₂ than outside air, but its PCO₂ (about 40 mmHg) is still below the blood's.

options.text: Into the alveolus, pumped out by the membrane
options.why: No pump: CO₂ crosses by simple diffusion, like O₂.

options.text: Nowhere: CO₂ leaves only through the kidneys
options.why: The lungs are the main exit for CO₂; it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides over a pass where the barometric pressure is 700 mmHg. Dry air is 20.9% O₂. What is the PO₂ of the dry air around her?

options.text: 146 mmHg
136 mmHg
options.why: This takes off water vapour first, 0.209 × (700 − 47). That is the PO₂ once air is humidified in the airways, not of the dry air outside.

options.text: 159 mmHg
options.why: That is the sea-level value. The O₂ share of air stays 20.9%, but the total pressure here is 700 mmHg, so PO₂ changes with it.

options.text: 14,630 mmHg
options.why: This multiplies by 20.9 instead of 0.209: turn the % into a fraction first.

variants.stem: A runner trains at altitude where the barometric pressure is 630 mmHg. Dry air is 20.9% O₂. What is the PO₂ of the dry air around him?

options.text: 132 mmHg
122 mmHg
options.why: This takes off water vapour first, 0.209 × (630 − 47). That is the PO₂ once air is humidified in the airways.

options.text: 159 mmHg
options.why: That is the sea-level value. The O₂ share of air stays 20.9%, but the total pressure here is 630 mmHg, so PO₂ changes with it.

options.text: 13,167 mmHg
options.why: This multiplies by 20.9 instead of 0.209.

variants.stem: On a stormy race day by the sea the barometric pressure is 740 mmHg. Dry air is 20.9% O₂. What is the PO₂ of the dry air around the triathletes?

options.text: 155 mmHg
145 mmHg
options.why: This takes off water vapour first, 0.209 × (740 − 47). That is the PO₂ once air is humidified in the airways.

options.text: 159 mmHg
options.why: That is the sea-level value. The O₂ share of air stays 20.9%, but the total pressure here is 740 mmHg, so PO₂ changes with it.

options.text: 15,466 mmHg
options.why: This multiplies by 20.9 instead of 0.209.

variants.stem: At rest, alveolar PO₂ is 104 mmHg and blood arriving in the lung capillary is at 40 mmHg. What is the PO₂ gradient driving O₂ into the blood?

options.text: 64 mmHg
options.why: Right: 104 − 40 = 64 mmHg.

options.text: 144 mmHg
options.why: This adds the two pressures; the gradient is their difference.

options.text: 4 mmHg
options.why: This uses blood leaving the lung (100 mmHg). The push acts on blood as it arrives, at 40 mmHg.

options.text: 2.6 mmHg
options.why: This divides 104 by 40. The gradient is a difference, in mmHg.

variants.solution: Gradient = alveolar PO₂ − arriving blood PO₂ = 104 − 40 = 64 mmHg.

variants.stem: Suppose that late in a hard run alveolar PO₂ rises to 115 mmHg and blood arriving in the lung capillary is down to 25 mmHg. What is the PO₂ gradient?

options.text: 90 mmHg
options.why: Right: 115 − 25 = 90 mmHg, a bigger push than the 64 mmHg at rest.

options.text: 140 mmHg
options.why: This adds the two pressures; the gradient is their difference.

options.text: 64 mmHg
options.why: That is the resting gradient. Both numbers have changed.

options.text: 4.6 mmHg
options.why: This divides 115 by 25. The gradient is a difference, in mmHg.

variants.stem: CO₂ crosses the alveolar wall with a gradient of only about 5 mmHg, against about 64 mmHg for O₂. What does that mean for the amounts that cross?

options.text: Similar amounts of the two gases still cross
options.why: Right: despite the small gradient, the amounts of O₂ and CO₂ that diffuse are similar.

options.text: Far less CO₂ crosses, so it builds up at rest
options.why: CO₂ doesn't build up at rest: the small gradient is enough to move it.

options.text: CO₂ needs an active pump to keep up
options.why: No pump is involved: CO₂ crosses by simple diffusion.

options.text: CO₂ crosses only once exercise widens the gradient
options.why: CO₂ crosses at rest too; a 5 mmHg gradient is enough.

variants.stem: Why does a red cell spend less time in a lung capillary during a hard ride than at rest?

options.text: Blood flow rises more than the capillary blood volume can grow
options.why: Right: transit time = capillary volume ÷ flow, and flow rises faster than the capillary volume is recruited.

options.text: The respiratory membrane gets thicker and slows it down
options.why: A thicker membrane would slow diffusion, not speed the blood. And the membrane doesn't thicken.

options.text: Faster breathing pushes the blood through the lungs
options.why: The heart drives lung blood flow; breathing rate doesn't set it.

options.text: Red cells shrink during exercise and slip through
options.why: Red-cell size doesn't change; it is more flow through a limited capillary volume.

variants.stem: A male recreational runner with a VO₂max of 45 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ races 5 km all out. Near the finish, what do you expect of his arterial PO₂?

options.text: Close to resting values, around 100 mmHg
options.why: Right: in most people ventilation and diffusion rise in step with metabolism, so arterial PO₂ holds.

options.text: Down by about 30 mmHg, as in any hard effort
options.why: Falls that large were seen in some highly trained runners, not in hard efforts in general.

options.text: Near 40 mmHg, like blood coming back from the legs
options.why: 40 mmHg is venous blood arriving in the lungs; arterial blood leaving them is far higher.

options.text: Near 159 mmHg, the PO₂ of outside air
options.why: Arterial PO₂ can't exceed alveolar PO₂ (about 104 mmHg), which is below that of outside air.

variants.stem: At the end of a maximal treadmill test, a runner's SaO₂ is 91%. How is that graded?

options.text: Moderate EIAH
options.why: Right: 88–93% is moderate.

options.text: Mild EIAH
options.why: Mild is 93–95% (or 3–4% below rest); 91% is lower.

options.text: Severe EIAH
options.why: Severe is below 88%.

options.text: Normal for maximal exercise
options.why: Most people hold SaO₂ near resting values; 91% is a clear fall.

variants.stem: At the end of a maximal cycling test, a rider's SaO₂ is 94%. How is that graded?

options.text: Mild EIAH
options.why: Right: 93–95% (or 3–4% below rest) is mild.

options.text: Moderate EIAH
options.why: Moderate is 88–93%; 94% is above that.

options.text: Severe EIAH
options.why: Severe is below 88%.

options.text: Normal for maximal exercise
options.why: A 3–4% fall from rest already counts as mild EIAH.

variants.stem: At the end of a maximal run, an elite triathlete's SaO₂ is 86%. How is that graded?

options.text: Severe EIAH
options.why: Right: below 88% is severe.

options.text: Moderate EIAH
options.why: Moderate is 88–93%; 86% is lower.

options.text: Mild EIAH
options.why: Mild is 93–95%.

options.text: Normal for maximal exercise
options.why: Most people hold SaO₂ near resting values; 86% is a large fall.

variants.stem: Which athlete is most likely to show EIAH at sea level?

options.text: A male runner with a VO₂max of 75 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, at the end of a maximal treadmill test
options.why: Right: EIAH is most common in highly trained athletes at maximal effort; 70% of such runners desaturated.

options.text: A recreational cyclist with a VO₂max of 40 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, on an easy ride
options.why: EIAH appears at heavy to maximal effort; an easy ride doesn't stress gas exchange.

options.text: A triathlete sitting at rest the day after a hard training block
options.why: EIAH is a fall during heavy exercise, not at rest.

options.text: A runner of any fitness, at 50% of VO₂max
options.why: At moderate effort ventilation and diffusion keep up in almost everyone.

variants.stem: Two things usually combine to cause EIAH. Which two?

options.text: A wide alveolar-to-arterial PO₂ gap and too little extra breathing
options.why: Right: an A-a gap above 25–30 mmHg plus weak hyperventilation (PaCO₂ above 35 mmHg) commonly combine.

options.text: Low haemoglobin and a thickened respiratory membrane
options.why: Neither is part of EIAH in healthy athletes; their haemoglobin and lungs are normal.

options.text: Asthma and breathing cold, dry air
options.why: Those can narrow airways, but EIAH occurs in healthy athletes without asthma.

options.text: Too much breathing and a low blood CO₂
options.why: Backwards: the problem is too little extra breathing, with PaCO₂ staying high.

variants.stem: A study reports that 70% of highly trained male runners show EIAH. It pooled 124 runners from one lab's past studies and estimated SaO₂ with an ear oximeter. What most limits that 70% figure?

options.text: SaO₂ was estimated, in men only, from past studies by one lab
options.why: Right: a retrospective, single-lab sample of men with oximeter estimates can't give a firm figure for all athletes.

options.text: 124 runners is too few to learn anything about EIAH
options.why: 124 is a large sample for this kind of study; the problems are the design and the measurement.

options.text: A treadmill test is easier than a cycling test
options.why: Not easier: the authors expected more desaturation on the treadmill, and mode is part of the question.

options.text: SaO₂ can't fall during exercise, so the result must be an error
options.why: SaO₂ can fall: blood-gas studies measured falls in arterial PO₂ directly.
